lines: Somebody finds a number that's been wrong for a while, long after it first went wrong.
The fix isn't retrying one record. It's running a whole stretch of history back through again.
And the very first question is where that second run's output should actually land.
One earlier fix handled a single stuck record, picked out on its own.
This is the same basic move, stretched across a whole slice of time instead.
And the starting point for that slice is simply a moment on a clock.
Worth reasoning through before the reveal settles it.
Say the fix means running everything back through, from the very first record this topic ever held.
Is that actually what has to happen, or is there a narrower way to do it?
answer: There's a narrower way, and it's usually the right one.
Only the specific slice that was actually wrong needs touching at all.
Everything outside that slice never needed fixing in the first place.

lines: Narrow it down to one lane, if that's the only one that was ever wrong.
Or narrow it down to a stretch of time, bounded on both ends.
Either way, nothing outside that boundary gets touched at all.
Sometimes that stretch of history isn't sitting in the fast, local copy anymore.
If it's still within how long the slower, cheaper copy sticks around, it's pulled from there instead.
Past that, it has to be put back together from wherever it already landed downstream.
Worth reasoning through once more before this reveal settles it.
Picture a second run of a fix landing its output right on top of the first, original numbers.
What does that quietly cost, once it's done?
answer: It costs the one thing anyone actually needed afterward.
The original numbers are simply gone, overwritten by the fix.
And without them, there's nothing left to check the fix actually worked.

lines: Land the fix right on top of the original, and the original stops existing.
There's no before to compare against anymore, only the after.
Whether the fix actually helped becomes a question nobody can answer.
Land it somewhere new instead, clearly marked apart from the original, and both survive.
Now the two can be set side by side, and walked back if the fix turns out wrong.
And anything that run would normally trigger out in the world gets told, plainly, not to fire again.
Every figure in this reel came from one real run, happening just now, of this topic's own toy models.
The jump straight to the right starting point, clean.
And the side-by-side proof: one run that erased its own history, and one that didn't.
So: start from a point in time, not a raw position nobody can reason about.
Touch only the slice that was actually wrong, never more than that.
And land the result somewhere new, with its side effects switched off, so fixing one mistake never risks making another.
